paras: The pursuit of the Fernandina jail escapees was a sheriffs' manhunt in late July 1895 near Fernandina, Florida, in which a posse fired on Black prisoners who had broken out of the Fernandina jail and drove them into the surf off Amelia beach. A widely reprinted wire dispatch reported that all four escapees, Tudor Brown, Willie Cook, Sam or Sim Echols and John Armstrong, drowned. A Florida weekly, however, reported that no one was found and judged drowning "hardly probable," so the coverage does not settle whether anyone died.

According to the wire dispatch, the four men broke jail at Fernandina on a Sunday night and hid in the scrub along the beach, while a South Carolina summary dated the break to Monday. The dispatch called them "desperate characters" and "negro outlaws," but none of the reports states what charges had put them in jail. Sheriff Higginbotham of Nassau County, the dispatch said, "determined to hunt them down."

The Bradford County Telegraph of Starke reported that three of the escaped men were surprised by a search party of Sheriff Higginbotham, Sheriff Bowden of Duval County and Sheriff Pons of Baker County in the scrub along Amelia beach, about five miles southeast of Fernandina. The men ran down the beach, ignored the order to halt and were fired upon, then plunged into the surf and were last seen heading seaward in the dark. The posse stayed on the beach until dawn without finding any of them, and the Starke paper concluded from a trail of blood to the water's edge that one man "had evidently been wounded." Carolina papers placed the chase on "late Thursday night" and said nothing had been found but a trail of blood and three hats.

The wire dispatch from Fernandina told the story differently. In its version all four men were found on the beach near Fort George and refused to surrender, after which the bloodhounds were loosed and the deputies "closed in and began firing." The men then rushed into the ocean, where they were "seen bobbing up and down on the waves" in the moonlight before they disappeared, and the dispatch reported them drowned.

No report of recovered bodies, an inquest or a recapture was found in the coverage. Writing a week after the drowning reports, the Starke weekly thought the men had swum out and let the tide carry them down the beach, and that "their escape was complete."

Most readers met the story as one sentence in syndicated weekly news summaries, printed August 1 to 3 in papers such as the Warren Sheaf (Minnesota), the Hope Pioneer (North Dakota) and the Perrysburg Journal (Ohio). That item, which several copies garbled to "Fernandila," stated flatly that the "negro desperadoes" had been "driven into the ocean by bloodhounds and all were drowned." Western papers including the Oregon Mist, the Pullman Herald and The Dalles Times-Mountaineer printed the longer dispatch under the headlines "Dashed Into the Ocean" and "Drowned Themselves," opening on "the bay of blood-hounds sounding nearer and nearer." Its dateline reads July 26 in the Dalles and Albany copies and July 29 in the Oregon Mist and Pullman Herald.

Southern papers were more cautious: the Winnsboro News and Herald and the Goldsboro Weekly Argus reported only that three men had been fired on and vanished into the sea, leaving blood and hats, and said nothing of deaths. The Bradford County Telegraph, the only Florida paper in the coverage, headed its account "Fired Upon the Fugitives" and openly doubted the drowning story. Every account came from the pursuers' side, none quoted the escaped men or anyone speaking for them, and no Black-press coverage of the episode was found.

The accounts conflict on how many men entered the water and whether they died: the wire dispatch put all four in the ocean and called them drowned, while the Carolina and Florida accounts put three on the beach and found no bodies, and the Florida paper said all "seemed to be expert swimmers." Bloodhounds appear only in the wire version and its summary. The Florida account is the only one from the state and the latest, published after the drowning reports.

reader.title: Pursuit of the Fernandina jail escapees
bases: A sheriffs' posse hunted escaped Black prisoners and fired on them as they fled into the surf; the wire version reports all four drowned (A6, A4), while the local Florida report doubts any died (A17), so the deaths are contested.

Independent versions agree that a sheriffs' posse fired on the escaped men on the beach and that they ran into the ocean (A2, A6, A17), but the wire dispatch's report that all four drowned (A6, A4) is contradicted by the Florida weekly, which found no bodies and judged drowning 'hardly probable' (A17).

accounts.label: Florida weekly (Starke)
accounts.gist: Three escapees were fired on by a search party of three sheriffs and swam out to sea; one was apparently wounded; the posse found no one by dawn, and the paper thought they escaped and that drowning was 'hardly probable'.

framing.detail: Northern and western weeklies ran the summary line calling the men 'negro desperadoes' and stating flatly that 'all were drowned'.

The full dispatch, headed 'Dashed Into the Ocean' or 'Drowned Themselves', told the chase dramatically ('the bay of bloodhounds sounding nearer') and called the men 'negro outlaws' and 'desperate characters'.
Southern news notes reported the firing and the blood trail without claiming deaths.
The Bradford County Telegraph headed its item 'Fired Upon the Fugitives' and judged the drowning story improbable.
